text: **Divine name.** Genesis 1 uses *Elohim* throughout (not YHWH), which I rendered "God." If you ever extend to Genesis 2+ where YHWH appears, you need a policy: HERE (AFR53 style), die HERE, Jahwe, Jehova, etc. This is a major translation decision.
Of: "Toe God begin skep het die hemel en die aarde …" — die Hebreeuse sintaksis laat albei lesings toe.

**Verse 1 — *bereshit bara Elohim*.** I went with "In die begin het God... geskep" (matches AFR53 tradition). A defensible alternative is "Toe God begin het om die hemel en die aarde te skep" — there's a real Hebrew grammatical argument for the latter.
"diepwater" vertaal die Hebreeuse *tehom* (die oer-dieptes).
**Verse 2 — *tohu wa-bohu*.** "Woes en leeg" is the AFR53/AFR83 convention. More literal would be "ongevormd en leeg" or "chaos en leegte."
**Verse 2 — *ruach Elohim*.** I rendered "Gees van God." This could also be "wind van God" or "magtige wind" (some modern translations). The Hebrew is genuinely ambiguous.
**Verse 2 — *tehom*.** "Diepwater" — could be "die dieptes" or "die oerwater." AFR53 uses "die wêreldvloed."
**Verses 6–8 — *raqia*.** "Uitspansel" follows tradition. The Hebrew literally means "beaten-out thing / dome." Modern translations sometimes use "gewelf" (vault).

**Verses 11–12 — botanical terms.** Hebrew distinguishes *deshe* (grass/vegetation), *eseb* (seed-bearing plants), and *etz pri* (fruit trees). I collapsed some of this; a careful translation would preserve the categories.
**Verse 21 — *tanninim*.** "Seediere" is mild. The word means "sea monsters / great sea creatures" — AFR53 uses "groot seediere," modern translations sometimes "see-ongediertes."
"Ons" — die meervoud van die Hebreeus word behou sonder om die betekenis hier vas te lê.
**Verse 26 — *na'aseh adam*.** "Laat Ons mense maak" — the plural "Ons" is preserved (theological loading: Trinity? royal plural? divine council?). I left it ambiguous as the Hebrew does.
**Verse 26 — *tselem* / *demut*.** "Beeld" / "gelykenis." Standard renderings; no controversy.

**Verses 27, 30 — *nephesh chayyah*.** I varied: "lewende wesens" in v.27 contexts, "lewende asem" in v.30. The Hebrew is the same phrase. A real translation would be consistent. **This is exactly the kind of drift I warned you about.**

**Verses 27, 30 — *nephesh chayyah*.** I varied: "lewende wesens" in v.27 contexts, "lewende asem" in v.30. The Hebrew is the same phrase. A real translation would be consistent. **This is exactly the kind of drift I warned you about.**

**Divine name — first use of YHWH.** Genesis 1 used only *Elohim* ("God"). From 2:4 onward the text uses the compound *YHWH Elohim* almost throughout. Per committed policy (`TRANSLATION_POLICY.md` § 3) this is rendered **"HERE God"** (all-caps HERE for the Tetragrammaton + "God" for Elohim). This is the first translated chapter to exercise the divine-name policy in practice. Plain *Elohim* in vv.1–3 stays "God".

**Verse 1 — *tseva'am*.** "hulle hele leërskare" (their whole host/array) — the heavenly bodies and all that fills the heavens and earth. Literal and traditional. A plainer alternative is "alles wat hulle bevat"; flagged for the reviewer's preference.
Die Masoretiese Teks lees "sewende dag"; die Samaritaanse Pentateug, Septuagint en Peshitta lees "sesde dag".

**Verse 2 — "op die sewende dag … voltooi": textual variant.** MT (WLC) reads that God finished "on the seventh day." The Samaritan Pentateuch, LXX and Peshitta read "on the **sixth** day" (harmonising away the apparent implication that God worked on the seventh). Per policy we **follow the MT** in the body and note the variant here. No change needed.
**Verse 2 — *melakhah* / *asah*.** *asah* → "gedoen/gemaak" (committed: *asah* = maak, distinct from *bara* = skep). Rendered "werk wat Hy gedoen het" for natural Afrikaans.

**Verse 3 — *bara … la'asot*.** Literally "which God created to make/do." Rendered "geskep het deur dit te maak." Note that **both** committed verbs appear together here (*bara* + *asah*); the distinction is preserved (skep / maak).

**Verse 4 — *toledot*.** "wordingsgeskiedenis" (account of origins). *toledot* is the structuring formula of Genesis ("these are the generations/account of…"); elsewhere it heads genealogies. A shorter "Dit is die geskiedenis van…" is also fine — flagged for register preference.
Die Hebreeuse woord *'ed* is onseker — "damp", of moontlik "ondergrondse stroom".

**Verse 6 — *'ed*.** Rendered "'n damp" (mist). The word is rare and disputed: "mist/vapour" (so older translations, via the versions) or "stream/subterranean spring" (so many modern scholars, via an Akkadian cognate *edû*). Genuinely uncertain — flagged for the theologian. If "stream" is preferred: "'n waterstroom het uit die aarde opgestyg."
Woordspel in die Hebreeus: die *mens* (*adam*) word uit die *grond* (*adamah*) gevorm.

**Verse 7 — *adam* / *adamah* wordplay.** The Hebrew puns: *ha-adam* (the human) is formed from the *adamah* (ground/soil). Afrikaans cannot reproduce the pun directly ("mens" / "grond"). Left naturalised; the connection is worth a printed footnote. Per glossary, *adam* stays the common noun **"die mens"** here (the *adam* → proper-name "Adam" decision is deferred to Genesis 4).

**Verse 7 — *yatsar*.** "geformeer" (the potter's verb). Committed glossary lists *yatsar* → "vorm/formeer" (🟡 provisional); I used **"geformeer"** consistently here and at v.8, v.19. Recommend committing "formeer". Distinct from *bara* (skep, 1:1; 2:3) and *asah* (maak).

**Verse 7 — *nephesh chayyah*.** "'n lewende wese" — per the now-committed *nephesh* context rule (creatures → "lewende wese"). Same phrase rendered identically at **v.19** (of the animals), deliberately consistent with Genesis 1 and avoiding the v.27/v.30 drift flagged in genesis-01.
**Verse 7 — *nishmat chayyim*.** "die asem van die lewe" (*neshamah*, breath). Distinct from *nephesh* (the living being that results) and from *ruach* (Gees/wind). Kept distinct in Afrikaans.
**Verse 8 — *miqqedem*.** "in die ooste" (spatial). Can also mean "of old / aforetime" (temporal). Most translations take the spatial sense given the geographic detail that follows. Noted.

**Verses 11–14 — proper names and minerals.** Per the proper-names policy, established Afrikaans geographic forms are used: **Tigris** and **Eufraat** (v.14) rather than transliterating *Chiddeqel* / *Perat*; **Kus** for *Kush* (v.13). Lesser names transliterated: **Pison**, **Gihon**, **Havila**. *bedolach* (v.12) → "balsemhars" (bdellium, an aromatic gum resin) and *shoham* → "onikssteen" — both mineral/resin identifications are uncertain; alternatives: bdellium left untranslated, *shoham* as "karneool/lapis". Flagged for the reviewer.

**Verses 18, 20 — *ezer kenegdo*.** "'n helper wat by hom pas" (a helper corresponding to / suitable for him). Avoided the loaded "hulp" alone and the archaic AFR53 "'n hulp wat by hom pas". *ezer* carries no subordinate connotation in Hebrew (it is used of God elsewhere); the rendering deliberately does not imply inferiority. Flagged for the theologian.

**Verses 18, 20 — *ezer kenegdo*.** "'n helper wat by hom pas" (a helper corresponding to / suitable for him). Avoided the loaded "hulp" alone and the archaic AFR53 "'n hulp wat by hom pas". *ezer* carries no subordinate connotation in Hebrew (it is used of God elsewhere); the rendering deliberately does not imply inferiority. Flagged for the theologian.

**Verse 20 — *ul'adam*.** "maar vir die mens" — the form is *l'adam* (without the article), which some read as the first occurrence of "Adam" as a proper name. Per the deferred *adam* decision (Genesis 4) I kept the common noun "die mens" for consistency within the chapter. Flag.

**Verses 21–22 — *tsela*.** "rib(be)". *tsela* usually means "side" (as in the side of the tabernacle); "rib" is the traditional rendering here and reads naturally. Noted; "rib" retained. *banah* (v.22, "to build") → "gebou", a slightly unusual verb deliberately preserved.
Woordspel in die Hebreeus: *vrou* (*ishshah*) is uit die *man* (*ish*) geneem.

**Verse 23 — *ishshah* / *ish* wordplay.** The pun ("she shall be called *ishshah* because she was taken from *ish*") survives partly in Afrikaans **vrou / man** but the sound-link is lost. AFR53 uses the archaic "manninne / man" to force it. I kept natural "vrou / man" and recommend a printed footnote explaining the Hebrew pun rather than distorting the Afrikaans. **Flagged** as a real choice for the team (this is the 🟡 item in `TRANSLATION_POLICY.md` § 6).

**Verse 25 — *arummim*.** "naak". Note the deliberate sound-play the author sets up with *arum* ("slu/listig", the serpent) in 3:1 — "naak" / "slu" does not carry it in Afrikaans. To be handled when Genesis 3 is translated; noted here so the wordplay is not lost across the chapter boundary.

**Divine name.** Narrative uses *YHWH Elohim* → **HERE God** (vv.8, 9, 13, 14, 21, 22, 23). Within speech the serpent and the woman say plain *Elohim* → **God** (vv.1, 3, 5), a deliberate contrast preserved here. Consistent with the policy established in Genesis 2.
"listig" (*arum*) speel in Hebreeus op "naak" (*arummim*, 2:25) — dieselfde klank verbind die mens se naaktheid en die slang se listigheid.

**Verse 1 — *arum*.** "listig" (crafty/shrewd). The word puns on *arummim* ("naked", 2:25); the sound-link is lost in Afrikaans and carried by the footnote (as flagged at the 2:25→3:1 boundary in genesis-02). Alternative "slu" is equally good; "listig" chosen as the more standard Afrikaans-Bible rendering for the serpent.

**Verse 1 — *af ki amar Elohim*.** "Het God werklik gesê…?" The particle *af ki* introduces the serpent's insinuating question; the distortion ("from *any/every* tree", *mikkol etz*) is preserved as "van al die bome", since the serpent overstates God's actual prohibition.

**Verses 3–4 — *temutun* / *lo mot temutun*.** The woman says "anders sal julle sterwe" (*pen temutun*); the serpent flatly negates God's 2:17 wording — "Julle sal sekerlik nie sterwe nie" (*lo mot temutun*), mirroring the emphatic *mot tamut* ("sekerlik sterwe") of 2:17. The contradiction is the point and is kept verbally parallel.
"soos God" (*ke'elohim*) kan ook "soos goddelike wesens / gode" beteken.
**Verse 5 — *ke'elohim*.** "soos God". Could be "like God" or "like divine beings/gods" (*Elohim* is morphologically plural); footnoted. The traditional singular "soos God" is retained in the body.
**Verse 6 — *lehaskil*.** "om insig te gee" (to make wise/prudent). Distinct from *chokmah* (wysheid); *haskil* is the verb of gaining insight/success.

**Verse 7 — *chagorot*.** "lendedoeke" (loincloths), chosen at review. *chagorah* (from *chagar*, "to gird") is a girdle/loincloth worn around the loins, so "lendedoek" is the literal rendering; preferred over the apron tradition ("skorte"/"voorskote") to stay true to the Hebrew. *eirummim* ("naak") echoes 2:25 and contrasts with the *arum* serpent of 3:1.
"in die aandwind" — letterlik "teen die wind (koelte) van die dag".

**Verse 8 — *leruach hayyom*.** "in die aandwind". *ruach* here is "wind/breeze" (per the glossary context rule, not "Gees"); *ruach hayyom* is idiomatically the cool evening breeze. Footnoted; AFR53 "teen die wind van die dag".
Tradisioneel as die eerste evangelie-belofte (die *protoevangelium*) gelees; "Hy" verwys na die nageslag. Dieselfde Hebreeuse werkwoord (*shuf*) staan by albei "vermorsel".

**Verse 15 — *shuf* (protoevangelium).** The **same** verb *yeshufekha* / *teshufennu* renders both clauses, so I used "vermorsel" for both to preserve the identity, even though "vermorsel die hakskeen" is slightly unusual in Afrikaans (some translations vary it to "byt/loer na" for the heel). The faithful single-verb rendering plus a footnote is the better choice — **confirmed at review**: stay true to the one Hebrew verb even where the Afrikaans is awkward (see the "fidelity over smoothness" principle in `TRANSLATION_POLICY.md` § 4). "Hy" (*hu*) refers grammatically to the collective *zera* ("nageslag"); left lowercase to avoid importing the messianic interpretation into the text (it is noted in the footnote instead).
"swaarkry" (*itstsavon*) is dieselfde woord wat in v.17 die man se straf beskryf — die vrou en die man se vonnis eggo mekaar. Die tweede woord, "pyn" (*etzev*), is die geboortepyn self.
"begeerte" (*teshuqah*) en "heers" — vergelyk dieselfde woordpaar in 4:7.

**Verse 16 — *itstsavon* / *etzev* / *teshuqah*.** *itstsavon* → **"swaarkry"**, rendered identically for the woman (v.16) and the man (v.17), so the deliberate word-link binding their two judgments is visible in the body (not buried in a footnote). *etzev* (v.16b, the actual birth labour — a sister noun of the same root ע־צ־ב) → **"pyn"**. "begeerte" for *teshuqah*; the *teshuqah* + "heers" (*mashal*) pairing recurs in 4:7 (sin's desire for Cain) and is kept identical so that cross-reference survives. The exact sense of v.16b is debated (desire "for" vs "against" the husband); the neutral "na jou man sal jou begeerte wees" is retained.

**Verses 17, 20–23 — *adam* / "die mens".** Kept as the common noun "die mens" throughout, even at *ul'adam* (v.17, anarthrous) where some read the first proper "Adam". Per the deferred decision (glossary: *adam* proper-name ruling at Genesis 4), consistency within the chapter is preserved; flagged for the Genesis 4 decision, which will likely back-name v.17/20–21 retroactively.
"Eva" (*Chawwa*) klink soos die Hebreeuse woord vir "lewe / lewende" (*chai*).

**Verses 17, 20–23 — *adam* / "die mens".** Kept as the common noun "die mens" throughout, even at *ul'adam* (v.17, anarthrous) where some read the first proper "Adam". Per the deferred decision (glossary: *adam* proper-name ruling at Genesis 4), consistency within the chapter is preserved; flagged for the Genesis 4 decision, which will likely back-name v.17/20–21 retroactively.
**Verse 20 — *Chawwa* / Eva.** "Eva" (established Afrikaans form). The naming puns on *chai* ("living") — "moeder van alle lewendes"; footnoted.

**Verse 22 — *ke'achad mimmennu*.** "soos een van Ons" — the divine plural again (cf. 1:26), left ambiguous as the Hebrew leaves it. The sentence breaks off (aposiopesis, *pen yishlach yado* …), rendered with an em-dash.

**Verse 24 — *keruvim* / *lahat hacherev*.** "gérubs" (cherubim, transliterated established form); "die vlam van die swaard wat heen en weer beweeg" for *lahat hacherev hammithappekhet* (the whirling/flashing sword). *gérubs* proposed for the glossary.

**Textual base.** I worked primarily from the Nestle-Aland 28 / UBS5 critical text. Where significant variants exist against the Textus Receptus (which underlies AFR53), I flag them below. **You need a policy on this for a full Bible** — pick one textual tradition and stay with it, or document every variant.
**Verse 1 — *Logos*.** "Woord" — universal Afrikaans convention. No controversy.

**Verse 1c — *theos en ho logos*.** "Die Woord was God." Anarthrous *theos* with definite *ho logos*. The Jehovah's Witness "a god" rendering is grammatically defensible but theologically minority; I followed the majority view. Worth knowing this exists.
"oorweldig" (*katelaben*) kan ook "begryp/aangryp" beteken; die Grieks is dubbelsinnig.

**Verse 5 — *katelaben*.** Can mean "overcome/master" or "grasp/comprehend." I went with "oorweldig" (overcome). AFR53 has "aangegryp." Both are defensible; the Greek is genuinely ambiguous and John may have intended both.

**Verse 9 — participle attachment.** *Erchomenon eis ton kosmon* ("coming into the world") could modify either "the light" or "every person." I attached it to the Light (modern consensus). AFR53 attaches it to "every person" ("elke mens wat in die wêreld kom"). **This is a real choice you need to commit to.**
"Enigste" vertaal *monogenēs* (uniek, een-van-'n-soort); tradisioneel "eniggebore".

**Verse 14 — *eskēnōsen*.** Literally "pitched a tent / tabernacled." I rendered "kom woon" which loses the Tabernacle/Exodus allusion. "Tent opgeslaan" would preserve it but reads strangely. AFR53 has "het onder ons gewoon."

**Verse 14, 18 — *monogenēs*.** Traditionally "eniggebore" (only-begotten); modern scholarship prefers "enigste" / "uniek" (unique/one-of-a-kind). I went with "Enigste." This is a real translation/theological choice with downstream implications.
Teksvariant: die kritiese teks lees "die Enigste — self God"; die Textus Receptus lees "die eniggebore Seun".

**Verse 14, 18 — *monogenēs*.** Traditionally "eniggebore" (only-begotten); modern scholarship prefers "enigste" / "uniek" (unique/one-of-a-kind). I went with "Enigste." This is a real translation/theological choice with downstream implications.

**Verse 18 — major textual variant.** NA28 reads *monogenēs theos* ("the only-begotten God / unique one, himself God"). TR reads *monogenēs huios* ("only-begotten Son"). AFR53 follows TR: "die eniggebore Seun." **I followed NA28 here**, which is why my rendering differs notably from what you'd expect. If you want to match AFR53/TR tradition, change to "die enigste Seun" or "die eniggebore Seun."
**Verse 27 — "I am not worthy."** I dropped the explicit "Ek" for natural Afrikaans flow. AFR53 keeps it.

**Verse 34 — textual variant.** NA28 has both *ho eklektos* ("the Chosen One") and *ho huios* ("the Son") well attested; modern translations split. AFR53/TR has "Seun." I went with "Seun" here to match likely reader expectation, but flagged it because **the same translator should not silently switch textual base between v.18 and v.34** — that's the kind of inconsistency that would embarrass you in production.
**Verse 41 — *prōton*.** Some manuscripts read *prōi* (early) instead of *prōton* (first). I took "first." Minor.
**Verse 51 — *amēn amēn*.** "Voorwaar, voorwaar" — AFR53 convention. Modern: "Ek verseker julle." I kept the traditional rendering.

**Textual base.** StatResGNT (critical text), now the committed NT base (`TRANSLATION_POLICY.md` § 2). John 2 has **no significant text-critical variants** affecting the translation, and none of the open glossary terms (*monogenēs*, *amēn amēn*) occur in this chapter, so it is a clean first chapter on the new committed base. Editorial markers in the source (`¶` paragraph marks, `˚` nomina-sacra marks before sacred names) were stripped before translating.

**Verse 1 — "op die derde dag".** *tē hēmera tē tritē* — literal "on the third day", counting from the events of 1:43ff. Kept literal; the resonance with the resurrection "third day" (cf. v.19) is the author's, not to be flattened.
**Verse 2 — *mathētai*.** "dissipels" (committed). Consistent throughout (vv.2, 11, 12, 17, 22).
"Vrou" (*gunai*) is 'n beleefde Griekse aanspreekvorm, al klink dit vreemd vir 'n seun teenoor sy moeder.

**Verse 4 — *gunai*.** "Vrou" — vocative *gunai* is courteous in Greek (not harsh), but a son addressing his mother as "Vrou" is striking in both Greek and Afrikaans, and the strangeness is deliberate in John. Retained literally rather than softened to "Moeder"; worth a footnote.

**Verse 4 — *ti emoi kai soi*.** Literally "what to Me and to you?" — a Semitic idiom marking distance/disengagement. Rendered "wat het Ek met u te doen?" (the standard Afrikaans idiomatic equivalent). Note the polite **"u"** for Jesus→Mary throughout, fitting the register.
**Verse 4 — *hē hōra mou*.** "My uur" — a loaded Johannine term (the hour of glorification/cross). Kept as the bare "uur"; the theological weight is carried by the term itself across the Gospel.
'n Metrete is ongeveer 39 liter; twee of drie elk ≈ 75–115 liter per kruik.

**Verse 6 — *metrētēs*.** Per the measurements policy (preserve source units + footnote), rendered "metrete" rather than converted to litres (committed at review). **Footnote for print:** a *metrētēs* ≈ 39 litres, so two-or-three each ≈ 75–115 litres per jar (~450–680 litres total).

**Verse 8 — *architriklinos*.** "seremoniemeester" (committed at review) — the master of the feast / head steward who ran the banquet, chosen over "tafelmeester"/"hoofkelner". Rendered consistently at vv.8, 9.

**Verse 10 — *methysthōsin*.** "dronk geword het" (committed at review). The verb's primary sense is "have become drunk"; the blunter rendering was chosen over the softer "volop gedrink het" to stay faithful to the proverb's literal force. The speaker is describing ordinary banquet practice, not passing moral judgement.

**Verses 11, 23 — *sēmeion*.** "teken" (sign), not "wonder/mirakel". This preserves John's characteristic theology of *signs* (events that signify who Jesus is). v.11 *archēn tōn sēmeiōn* → "eerste van die tekens". Proposed as committed glossary term below. *doxa* → "heerlikheid" (committed).

**Verse 13 — *Pascha*.** "Pasga" (the Jewish Passover), deliberately **not** "Paasfees", which in Afrikaans usage collides with Easter. Consistent at vv.13, 23. Committed at review as a Gospel-wide convention.

**Verses 14–16 vs 19–21 — *hieron* / *naos*.** John uses **two** temple words and the distinction matters here. *hieron* (the whole temple precincts, where trade happened) at vv.14, 15 and *naos* (the sanctuary proper) at vv.19, 20, 21 are **both** rendered "tempel" per the current glossary, because Afrikaans has no natural lexical pair. The wordplay — Jesus speaks of the *naos* as His body — is therefore **flagged for a footnote**. This is exactly the *hieron* 🟡 item in `GLOSSARY.md`; recommend keeping a single "tempel" rendering + footnote rather than forcing a distinction like "tempelgebou/heiligdom".
Die aanhaling is Psalm 69:9; voorlopig uit die Grieks vertaal totdat ons eie Psalm 69 beskikbaar is.

**Verse 17 — OT quotation (Ps 69:9).** "Die ywer vir u huis sal My verteer." **Committed policy** (`TRANSLATION_POLICY.md` § 2 #8 + § 2a): NT quotations of the OT are rendered **to match our own OT translation**. Psalm 69 is not yet translated, so this is rendered **provisionally from the Greek** and entered on the back-harmonisation list in `REVIEW_LOG.md` — to be conformed to our Afrikaans Ps 69:9 once the Psalms are done. Note for that pass: John follows the LXX of Ps 69:9 (future "sal verteer / *kataphagetai*") against the MT's "has consumed"; preserve our OT wording in the body and footnote the divergence if the difference is material.
"tempel": hier *naos* (die heiligdom self), teenoor *hieron* (die hele tempelterrein) in vers 14 — Jesus bedoel sy liggaam.

**Verse 22 — *graphē* / *logos*.** "Skrif" and "woord". Here *logos* is the ordinary "statement Jesus made", **not** the Christological *Logos* of John 1:1 — so lowercase "woord", deliberately distinct from the capital-W "Woord" reserved for Christ. Noted to prevent false consistency.

**Verses 11, 23 — *sēmeion*.** "teken" (sign), not "wonder/mirakel". This preserves John's characteristic theology of *signs* (events that signify who Jesus is). v.11 *archēn tōn sēmeiōn* → "eerste van die tekens". Proposed as committed glossary term below. *doxa* → "heerlikheid" (committed).

**Verses 23–24 — *episteusan* / *episteuen* wordplay.** John puns: many "believed/trusted" (*episteusan*, v.23) in Him, but Jesus did not "entrust" (*episteuen*, v.24) Himself to them — the same verb *pisteuō*. Rendered "geglo" (v.23) / "toevertrou" (v.24); the pun is partly lost in Afrikaans. Noted; a footnote could flag it.
